Se adoptan los criterios Duke-ISCVID de 2023 como referencia diagnóstica actual, con diagnóstico molecular en los criterios anatomopatológicos, lista ampliada de microorganismos típicos, microorganismos «situacionalmente típicos» asociados a material protésico, nuevas modalidades de imagen y un criterio mayor quirúrgico por inspección operatoria de la válvula infectada; se eliminan los criterios ecocardiográficos menores. Son más sensibles que los criterios de Duke modificados de 2000, con reducción nula o modesta de la especificidad; frente a los criterios diagnósticos de la ESC de 2023 tienen sensibilidad similar y mayor especificidad, aunque en la bacteriemia enterocócica ganan sensibilidad (79% frente a 74%) a costa de especificidad (55% frente a 69%).

La imagen se estructura en tres niveles. La ecocardiografía sigue siendo la primera línea: la transtorácica tiene especificidad >90% pero sensibilidad del 40% al 66%, y del 20% al 46% para complicaciones perivalvulares, por lo que se realiza ecocardiografía transesofágica en portadores de válvula protésica o de dispositivo aunque la transtorácica sea negativa, y en válvula nativa con probabilidad pretest intermedia o alta. La PET/TC con 18F-fluorodesoxiglucosa se apoya como herramienta adyuvante de segunda línea en la sospecha de endocarditis protésica con ecocardiografía negativa o no concluyente (sensibilidad >80%-90% en protésica, especificidad similar), con sensibilidad baja en válvula nativa, y requiere dieta cetogénica rica en grasas y pobre en hidratos durante las 24 horas previas. La SPECT/TC con leucocitos marcados queda para cuando la PET/TC no está disponible.

La tomografía computarizada cardíaca se consolida para las complicaciones paravalvulares y periprotésicas cuando la ecocardiografía no es concluyente, y como alternativa a la coronariografía invasiva para descartar enfermedad coronaria proximal significativa en pacientes de riesgo bajo o intermedio antes de la cirugía. La resonancia magnética cerebral es superior a la tomografía en el paciente con síntomas neurológicos y es razonable en el asintomático que va a cirugía cardíaca; la detección de émbolos isquémicos silentes no es motivo para retrasar la intervención.

La terapia oral parcial deja de ser una excepción: se considera una opción para pacientes seleccionados tras la fase aguda, y no un tratamiento inferior o de segunda línea. Los criterios de paso a la vía oral son explícitos: endocarditis por estreptococos, Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus aureus sensible a meticilina o estafilococos coagulasa negativos; al menos 10 días de antibiótico intravenoso adecuado y al menos 7 días tras la cirugía valvular; estabilidad clínica con ausencia de fiebre durante al menos 3 días, proteína C reactiva <25% del valor pico o <20 mg/L y leucocitos <15×10⁹/L; y ecocardiografía transesofágica en los 2 días previos al cambio, sin progresión de la infección, sin absceso y sin nueva indicación quirúrgica. No se alcanzó consenso sobre si la pauta oral debe ser doble o en monoterapia.

Los lipoglucopéptidos inyectables de acción prolongada entran como alternativa para pacientes seleccionados en los que la vía intravenosa diaria es inviable y la vía oral no es opción, con pautas habituales de dalbavancina de 1.500 mg los días 1 y 8 o 3.000 mg repartidos en 4 semanas, y de oritavancina de 1.200 mg semanales. Los avisos también son nuevos: alto coste, uso fuera de ficha técnica en endocarditis, tasa de recaída del 8% en la endocarditis por E. faecalis (15% en la protésica), casos descritos de resistencia cruzada con vancomicina y daptomicina, y prolongación de las pruebas de coagulación por la oritavancina, que contraindica la heparina no fraccionada intravenosa durante 120 horas.

Caen varios tratamientos adyuvantes clásicos. En la endocarditis protésica estafilocócica se alcanzó consenso en que el riesgo de la gentamicina supera cualquier posible beneficio, mientras que sobre la rifampicina no hubo consenso y se remite la decisión al equipo de endocarditis. En la endocarditis por estreptococos del grupo viridans o Streptococcus gallolyticus con resistencia intermedia a penicilina se alcanzó consenso a favor de la ceftriaxona en monoterapia, reservando la gentamicina de las dos primeras semanas para los aislados plenamente resistentes a penicilina. Y en la endocarditis estafilocócica sobre válvula nativa que se opera, se considera razonable continuar en monoterapia en lugar de pasar al régimen de válvula protésica. Se mantiene, en cambio, el tratamiento combinado en la endocarditis por E. faecalis, y se considera razonable la colonoscopia en la endocarditis por E. faecalis o S. gallolyticus para descartar neoplasia colónica.

Se reescribe la duración del tratamiento en torno a la cirugía: no es necesario completar la antibioterapia antes de operar; los días preoperatorios cuentan para el total de 4 a 6 semanas, con un mínimo de 14 días postoperatorios y sin «reiniciar el reloj» tras la intervención. El cultivo positivo de la válvula resecada o la positividad de las pruebas moleculares no prolongan por sí mismos el tratamiento, y si el paciente completó la pauta antes de operarse sin signos de infección activa y con cultivos valvulares negativos, no se necesitan antibióticos postoperatorios. En cuanto al momento de operar, una vez establecida la indicación durante la fase activa se prefiere la cirugía precoz en 48 a 72 horas, salvo ictus mayor o hemorragia cerebral: el ictus hemorrágico obliga a demorar al menos 2 semanas y preferiblemente 4, y no se opera al paciente en coma. Como técnica emergente, la aspiración mecánica percutánea se recoge para casos seleccionados de endocarditis tricuspídea o sobre cables de dispositivo con alto riesgo quirúrgico en los que ha fracasado el tratamiento médico, sin datos de ensayos aleatorizados que la respalden.
es.conclusiones: Para el cardiólogo clínico general el mensaje operativo es que la endocarditis deja de manejarse en solitario: el documento sitúa el equipo de endocarditis como la vía normal de decisión y lo asocia a mejor mortalidad a corto plazo y a más cirugía y más precoz, de modo que la tarea del clínico de primera línea es activarlo pronto y no gestionar en paralelo. En el diagnóstico, conviene tener el umbral bajo para la ecocardiografía transesofágica —obligada en prótesis y dispositivos aunque la transtorácica sea negativa— y saber que la PET/TC y la tomografía cardíaca ya no son curiosidades sino criterios mayores en la endocarditis protésica. En el tratamiento, la vía oral parcial y los lipoglucopéptidos de acción prolongada permiten sacar antes del hospital a pacientes seleccionados que cumplan los criterios de estabilización, incluida la transesofágica previa al cambio. Y hay tres gestos concretos que cambian desde hoy: no añadir gentamicina en la endocarditis protésica estafilocócica, no reiniciar el cómputo antibiótico tras la cirugía valvular, y pedir colonoscopia ante una endocarditis por E. faecalis o S. gallolyticus. Conviene recordar que son sugerencias sin clase ni nivel de evidencia, con consenso explícito en unos puntos y ausencia de consenso en otros.

en.resumen: New American Heart Association scientific statement on infective endocarditis, replacing the 2015 document. It adopts the 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria, incorporates molecular diagnostics and multimodality imaging, gives formal standing to partial oral therapy and long-acting lipoglycopeptides, removes adjunctive gentamicin from staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis, and places the endocarditis team at the centre of every decision.
en.why: this is the reference US update of a document untouched for eleven years, and it arrives in a transformed landscape: incidence has risen, epidemiology has changed — ageing, intracardiac devices, prosthetic material and injection drug use-related endocarditis — and diagnostic and therapeutic tools have appeared that did not exist in 2015. What moves practice is mostly therapeutic: partial oral therapy is no longer an exception and is defined by explicit stabilisation criteria; long-acting lipoglycopeptides enter as an alternative for patients who cannot keep a line; adjunctive gentamicin falls by consensus in staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis; ceftriaxone monotherapy is accepted in viridans group streptococci with intermediate penicillin resistance; and the antibiotic clock is no longer restarted after valve surgery. One change of format is worth knowing: unlike the 2015 document, this statement issues no formal recommendations with class or level of evidence but management suggestions, and states explicitly where the writing group reached consensus and where it did not.
en.deque: American Heart Association scientific statement published online in Circulation on 8 September 2026, produced by an international writing group of twelve experts in cardiovascular infections chaired by Daniel C. DeSimone and endorsed by the International Society for Cardiovascular Infectious Diseases and the Canadian Cardiovascular Society. It replaces the 2015 AHA scientific statement on infective endocarditis in adults and is aimed at front-line clinicians managing complex cases that often fall outside existing guidelines: cardiology, cardiovascular surgery, infectious diseases, microbiology, neurology, radiology, pharmacy and nursing. It is complemented by four focused AHA scientific statements — prevention (2021), endocarditis in people who inject drugs (2022), cardiac implantable electronic device infections (2024) and blood culture-negative endocarditis (2025) — and by three science advisories on nondental invasive procedures (2023), selected nonvalvular cardiovascular device infections (2026) and percutaneous mechanical aspiration in right-sided endocarditis (2026). Its guidance is expressly framed as supporting, rather than supplanting, individual decisions ideally made with a multidisciplinary endocarditis team.
resultados: The format changes from 2015: unlike that statement and its predecessors, this document issues no formal diagnostic and treatment recommendations with class and level of evidence, but management suggestions, and states at each controversial point whether the writing group reached consensus. The reason is the scarcity of randomised trials: only one trial of antimicrobial therapy in endocarditis with adequate size and follow-up has been conducted, the POET trial, published after 2015.

The endocarditis team becomes the axis of management: a multispecialty team is endorsed, comprising cardiology with imaging expertise, cardiovascular surgery, infectious diseases, clinical microbiology, neurology, primary care, radiology, dentistry, pharmacy and nursing, with addiction medicine essential in people who inject drugs. A systematic review and meta-analysis associated dedicated multidisciplinary teams with improved short-term mortality, decreased time to surgery and an increased rate of surgery.

The 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria are adopted as the contemporary diagnostic reference, with molecular diagnostics in the pathologic criteria, an expanded list of typical pathogens, 'situationally typical' organisms associated with prosthetic material, new imaging modalities and a new major surgical criterion for operative inspection of the infected valve; echocardiographic minor criteria are eliminated. They are more sensitive than the 2000 modified Duke criteria with a null to modest reduction in specificity; against the 2023 ESC diagnostic criteria they have similar sensitivity and higher specificity, although in enterococcal bacteraemia they gain sensitivity (79% versus 74%) at the expense of specificity (55% versus 69%).

Imaging is structured in three tiers. Echocardiography remains first line: transthoracic echocardiography has specificity >90% but sensitivity of 40% to 66%, and 20% to 46% for perivalvular complications, so transoesophageal echocardiography is performed in patients with prosthetic valves or devices even if transthoracic imaging is negative, and in native valves when pretest probability is intermediate or high. 18F-FDG-PET/CT is supported as a second-line adjunctive tool in suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis when echocardiography is negative or inconclusive (sensitivity >80%-90% in prosthetic valve endocarditis, with similar specificity), with low sensitivity in native valve disease, and requires a high-fat, low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet for 24 hours beforehand. White blood cell SPECT/CT is reserved for when PET/CT is unavailable.

Cardiac computed tomography is consolidated for paravalvular and periprosthetic complications when echocardiography is inconclusive, and as an alternative to invasive angiography to exclude clinically significant proximal coronary artery disease in low- and intermediate-risk patients before surgery. Brain MRI is superior to CT in patients with neurologic symptoms and is reasonable in the asymptomatic patient going to cardiac surgery; detection of silent ischaemic emboli is not a reason to delay the operation.

Partial oral therapy is no longer an exception: it is an option for select patients after the acute phase, and is not considered inferior or second-line therapy. The criteria for switching to oral treatment are explicit: endocarditis due to streptococci, Enterococcus faecalis, methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus or coagulase-negative staphylococci; at least 10 days of appropriate intravenous antimicrobials and at least 7 days after valve surgery; clinical stability with no fever for at least 3 days, C-reactive protein <25% of peak value or <20 mg/L and leukocytes <15×10⁹/L; and transoesophageal echocardiography within 2 days of the switch, without evidence of infection progression, abscess formation or a new indication for surgery. No consensus was reached on whether the oral regimen should be dual or monotherapy.

Long-acting injectable lipoglycopeptides enter as an alternative for select patients in whom daily intravenous therapy is not feasible and oral therapy is not an option, with common dalbavancin regimens of 1,500 mg on days 1 and 8 or a total of 3,000 mg over 4 weeks, and oritavancin 1,200 mg weekly. The caveats are equally new: high cost, off-label use in endocarditis, an 8% relapse rate in E faecalis endocarditis (15% in prosthetic valve disease), reported cross-resistance with vancomycin and daptomycin, and prolongation of coagulation assays by oritavancin, which contraindicates intravenous unfractionated heparin for 120 hours.

Several classic adjunctive treatments fall away. In staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis, consensus was reached that the risk of gentamicin outweighs any potential benefit, whereas no consensus was reached on rifampin and the decision is referred to the endocarditis team. In endocarditis due to viridans group streptococci or Streptococcus gallolyticus with intermediate resistance to penicillin, consensus was reached in favour of ceftriaxone monotherapy, reserving two weeks of gentamicin for fully penicillin-resistant isolates. And in staphylococcal native valve endocarditis that goes to surgery, continuing monotherapy rather than switching to a prosthetic valve regimen appears reasonable. Combination therapy is retained in E faecalis endocarditis, and colonoscopy is considered reasonable in E faecalis or S gallolyticus endocarditis to evaluate for colonic malignancy.

Treatment duration around surgery is rewritten: completion of antimicrobial therapy before operating is not required; preoperative days count towards the planned 4- to 6-week course, with a minimum of 14 days postoperatively and without 'restarting the clock' after the operation. A positive resected valve culture or positive molecular testing does not in itself prolong therapy, and if the patient completed the course before surgery with no signs of active infection and negative valve tissue cultures, no additional postoperative antibiotics are needed. As for timing, once the indication is established during the active phase, early surgery within 48 to 72 hours is favoured, unless there has been a major stroke or cerebral haemorrhage: haemorrhagic stroke usually delays surgery at least 2 weeks and preferably 4, and cardiac surgery is not appropriate in comatose patients. As an emerging technique, percutaneous mechanical aspiration is described for select patients with tricuspid valve or device lead-related endocarditis and high surgical risk in whom medical therapy has failed, with no randomised trial data to support it.
en.conclusiones: For the general clinical cardiologist the operational message is that endocarditis is no longer managed alone: the document makes the endocarditis team the normal route to decisions and links it to better short-term mortality and to more, and earlier, surgery, so the front-line clinician's task is to activate it early rather than manage in parallel. In diagnosis, the threshold for transoesophageal echocardiography should be low — mandatory in prosthetic valves and devices even if the transthoracic study is negative — and PET/CT and cardiac CT are no longer curiosities but major criteria in prosthetic valve endocarditis. In treatment, partial oral therapy and long-acting lipoglycopeptides allow selected patients who meet the stabilisation criteria, including the transoesophageal study before the switch, to leave hospital earlier. And three concrete gestures change from today: do not add gentamicin in staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis, do not restart the antibiotic count after valve surgery, and request colonoscopy in E faecalis or S gallolyticus endocarditis. It is worth remembering that these are suggestions without class or level of evidence, with explicit consensus on some points and none on others.
